alkjnaNNasz.title: The Mirror of Self-Criticism
alkjnaNNasz.statement: Imagine saying all those critical thoughts you usually direct at yourself to your best friend. This exercise helps you see how unfair self-criticism can be and teaches you to treat yourself with more warmth, support, and understanding.
task: 1️⃣ Choose a situation where you often become self-critical.
2️⃣ Imagine that a close friend or someone dear to you was in that exact same situation.
3️⃣ Role-play the scene: stay as yourself, while your imaginary interlocutor is your friend.
4️⃣ Say out loud the critical phrases you usually say to yourself, but direct them toward your “friend.”
Pay attention to how you feel while doing this. Is it easy for you to say such things to someone else?
Notice the difference between how you treat yourself and how you treat others in similar situations.
Think about how you would actually support a friend. What would you say to them?
Now, try to show yourself that same level of care, understanding, and support.
example: Your usual thoughts about yourself:
I’m a total failure. Of course I didn’t get the promotion — I’m incompetent. I’ll probably never succeed in my career. I’m not smart or talented enough for this job.
Now imagine your best friend, Anna, didn’t get the promotion and told you about it. Try saying those same words to her:
Anna, you’re a total failure. Of course you didn’t get the promotion — you’re incompetent. You’ll probably never succeed in your career. You’re not smart or talented enough for this job.
How do you feel saying this to Anna? You’ll likely feel awkward and uncomfortable saying such things.
Now, think about what you would actually say to Anna:

Anna, I’m so sorry you didn’t get the promotion. I know how much effort you put in. It’s really disappointing, but it doesn’t make you a failure. You have so many strengths and achievements. Maybe it’s just not the right time, or there are a few skills you could develop further. Let’s think about how you can keep growing in your career.

Now, try saying these words of support to yourself. Notice how differently you treat yourself compared to a loved one in the same situation. Practice this exercise regularly to gradually learn how to treat yourself with the same kindness.
expectations: Realizing that self-criticism is often unjustified and excessive
Improved self-esteem and confidence
Reduced stress and anxiety levels

asgNldsc.title: Pay attention to your inner state
asgNldsc.statement: Learn to notice and name your feelings in the present moment.
description: This is a simple exercise to help you prepare for deeper mindfulness practices.
Its goal is to step out of the stream of thoughts and gently shift your attention to your emotions.
These exercises develop your ability to focus. Most of our experiences are tied to the past or the future, and by returning to the present moment, we can reduce the impact of anxious emotions.
task: A few times a day, take short breaks and shift your attention from your thoughts to your emotions.
Notice any feelings that arise and simply give them a name.
For example:
I feel a little sad
I feel tension
I’m starting to feel irritated
Avoid holding onto emotions or trying to change them. Just let them pass gently through the space of your attention.
expectations: Each time you do this, it will become easier to notice your emotions.
Emotions will have less of an impact on how you feel, as you’ll be meeting them mindfully.
This exercise will prepare you for deeper mindfulness techniques.

dfdzsWz4nJ.title: Notice 3 things
dfdzsWz4nJ.statement: Shift your attention from anxious thoughts to the present moment.
description: This is a simple exercise to help you prepare for deeper mindfulness practices.
Its goal is to step out of the stream of thoughts and gently focus on the here and now.
These exercises develop your ability to sustain attention. Often, our experiences are tied to the past or the future, and by returning to the present moment, we can reduce their influence on us.
example: While in a familiar place, find 3 things 🏡 that you haven’t noticed before. Focus fully on each one, one by one.
🕗 Spend 2–3 minutes on the exercise.
After that, take a short pause and try to maintain your focus for another 2–3 minutes. Try to do this exercise at least 10 times throughout the day.
expectations: Over time, it will become easier for you to stay present.
Your anxiety levels will gradually decrease.
This exercise will prepare you for more advanced mindfulness techniques.

kdzYJ4njVJ.title: Three Scenarios
kdzYJ4njVJ.statement: This technique helps your brain see different possible outcomes of a situation. You’ll learn to challenge negative thoughts and reduce anxiety.
description: We often judge situations too categorically, which prevents us from seeing the full picture. This exercise helps you return to a more objective perspective.
task: When you notice an anxious automatic thought, ask yourself: what are the possible ways this could unfold:
the worst — the most negative and frightening scenario that comes to mind first;
the best — the ideal outcome that would satisfy you completely;
the realistic — the most likely scenario, based on your experience and the facts;
Write these scenarios down in the app or on paper — it helps you better understand your thoughts and track changes.
example: Imagine you have an important exam tomorrow, and the thought arises: “I’m going to fail.” It’s unpleasant, but we can offer your brain an alternative.
❤️ Worst-case scenario
I’ll panic, won’t be able to remember anything, and will fail the exam. The teacher will be disappointed, and my classmates will think I’m lazy and incapable.
💜 Best-case scenario
I’ll stay calm, get easy questions, and pass the exam with flying colors. Or everyone will get the highest grade at once.
💚 Realistic scenario
I don’t know what the questions will be, but I can prepare a bit more and feel more confident. It’s okay to be nervous. Overall, I know the material well and will be able to answer most questions.
expectations: A more objective perception of situations
Reduced anxiety and emotional tension

lsafnanS3sf.title: Day Under Control
lsafnanS3sf.statement: This technique is helpful for people dealing with depression or procrastination. It can help you improve your organization and manage your time more effectively.
description: In the evening, before the next day begins, sit down and write out your schedule.
In the basic version, we suggest using 4 columns:
1️⃣ The first column is “Time.” The approximate time for a task. This can be a time interval.

2️⃣ The second column is “To Do.” This is an hourly plan of what you want to achieve. Don’t try to write too much at once: in each hourly row, write just one or two words to indicate an activity or action.

For example, it could be something small: take a shower, eat breakfast, or start a load of laundry. Or it could be something more demanding: cleaning 🧹, studying for an exam 🧪, writing a resume ✍🏼, etc.
3️⃣ At the end of each day, fill in the third column — “After.”
Use this to record what you actually did throughout the day. Your activities might match your plan, or they might be different — that’s okay, don’t worry about it.
Even if you only manage to complete a small part of your “To Do” list, simply planning your day can be a very helpful and visually clear process.
4️⃣ The fourth column is “Enjoyment.” You can find satisfaction even in routine tasks.
Most importantly, the mere fact of moving forward brings a sense of pleasure. On a scale of 1 to 10, rate how pleasant it was to complete the task.
task: In the evening, before the next day begins, sit down and write out your schedule.
In the basic version, we suggest using 4 columns:
1️⃣ The first column is “Time.” The approximate time for a task. This can be a time interval.
2️⃣ The second column is “To Do.” This is an hourly plan of what you want to achieve.
3️⃣ At the end of each day, fill in the third column — “After.”
Use this to record what you actually did throughout the day.
4️⃣ The fourth column is “Enjoyment.” On a scale of 1 to 10, rate how pleasant it was to complete the task.

2: Talked to a friend on the phone

expectations: It can reduce the tendency to constantly overthink the importance or value of certain actions and help you resolve internal conflicts about whether or not something is worth doing.
It will help you plan your time in a more balanced way, as it will include both necessary tasks and activities that bring you joy.
If you make a schedule regularly, you’ll soon notice your motivation growing; by starting to do even small things, you’ll challenge the belief that you are incapable of getting things done.

lsvnnDSnsdl.title: Embracing the possibility of mistakes
lsvnnDSnsdl.statement: The fear of making mistakes is a common companion to perfectionism. This technique will help you learn to accept mistakes more calmly.
task: Mistakes are unpleasant for everyone, but for perfectionists, they can become a true source of anxiety.
One of the most effective ways to ease the fear of imperfection is to learn to accept the possibility of making mistakes.
Try writing a short essay on why mistakes are a natural part of the journey, and why the pursuit of absolute perfection is both unattainable and exhausting.
example: Your thoughts might be something like:
The fear of making a mistake comes from black-and-white thinking: as if one mistake could undo all my efforts. But that’s not true. One small mistake doesn’t cancel out everything good I’ve done.
Mistakes provide us with experience and are the foundation of learning. No one is immune to mistakes, and it’s important to learn to accept them and keep moving forward.
When we acknowledge our mistakes, we can adjust our behavior and become more effective. This builds confidence and improves our quality of life.
Most people don’t judge us for our mistakes or stop loving us—everyone makes mistakes, and many people find it much more comfortable to be around real, living people rather than “perfect” ones.
expectations: You will feel calmer about your own mistakes.
Mistakes will be perceived as part of your growth rather than a catastrophe.

naslSLnadfl.title: Mistake Acceptance Worksheet
naslSLnadfl.statement: Many perfectionists believe that enjoyment is only possible when the result is perfect. Let’s gently challenge 💪 this belief.
description: High standards can be motivating, but when expectations become unrealistic, they turn into a trap: self-criticism intensifies, feelings of inadequacy arise, and emotional exhaustion sets in.
Absolute perfection doesn’t exist, and striving for it inevitably leads to frustration.
This technique helps you see that enjoyment comes from the process, not just the perfection of the result. Try completing a task imperfectly, but with interest and pleasure. Notice how you feel.
task: 1️⃣ For a few days, write down any tasks you perform: “brushing teeth,” “cooking dinner,” “writing a report,” “cleaning the house”—anything at all.
2️⃣ In the second column, indicate how effectively you think you handled the task (as a percentage).
3️⃣ In the third, note your level of enjoyment while doing the task.

0: 90% (simple, tasty, and didn’t take much time)
1: 70% (did the main things, didn’t get to the details)
2: 20% (perfectionism made it hard to enjoy it)

expectations: You will see that enjoyment isn’t necessarily tied to perfection.
Your anxiety and fear of making mistakes will decrease.

sdfcgNldslm.title: Mindful eating: rediscover flavor
sdfcgNldslm.statement: Learn to be present during every meal and discover familiar foods in a whole new way.
description: In the rush of daily life, we often eat on autopilot, barely noticing the taste. This exercise helps you slow down and truly feel the process.
You’ll learn to mindfully notice taste, smell, texture, and the emotions that arise.
Mindful eating allows you to savor every bite, turning an ordinary meal into a deep sensory experience.
task: Take a small piece of food 🍇, like a raisin or a nut. Hold it in your hand and feel its weight. Close your eyes and try to sense how light or heavy it is.
Observe closely 👀: open your eyes and look at the food as if you’re seeing it for the first time. What do you notice? Its shape, color, or how the light hits it?
Touch 🤲: feel the texture—is it smooth or rough? Try using different fingers; do the sensations change?
Smell 👃: notice the aroma. Is it fresh, sweet, or intense? Does it bring back any memories?
Taste 👅: place the piece on your tongue and resist the urge to chew immediately. Notice how the flavor changes with every passing second.
Swallow 👄: feel the food as you swallow and notice the sensations that linger afterward.
expectations: Each time, you’ll find yourself sinking deeper into the experience of eating.
You’ll notice subtle nuances of taste and texture that you might have missed before.
This practice helps reduce stress, encourages you to slow down, and helps you find beauty in simple moments.

DzseWuFv2t.title: Standing up to your inner critic
DzseWuFv2t.statement: Feelings of inadequacy are often driven by an inner critic that undermines your self-esteem. This technique helps you learn how to respond to that criticism and reframe unhelpful thoughts.
description: Thoughts like “I’m worthless,” “I’m worse than others,” “I’ll never succeed,” “It’s all my fault,” or “I’m a failure” can lower your self-esteem and lead to depressive experiences.
It’s important not to give in to your inner critic and to learn how to calmly talk back to it. This helps you develop a fairer and kinder view of yourself.
task: Create a table with three columns. Name the columns:
Critic’s thoughts
Cognitive distortion
Rational response
1️⃣ In the first column, write down the self-critical thoughts that arise when you feel guilty, useless, or dissatisfied with yourself.
It’s important to record thoughts, not feelings. For example, the phrase “I feel bad” cannot be refuted because the feeling is already there.
2️⃣ In the second column, identify the cognitive distortion behind the thought.
3️⃣ In the third column, formulate a calm, rational response to the critic. Try to find a logical and supportive explanation.
Try to replace self-criticism with realistic and kind thoughts, while avoiding excessive optimism.
example: Here are a few examples of rational responses:

0: I’m so stupid, I’ll definitely fail
I’m not stupid; I just haven’t finished preparing everything yet. If I keep studying, I have a high chance of passing.
1: There are people who value and love me. I am important to those close to me.
2: I’ll never be able to find a job
I can find a job if I keep looking and growing. Many people go through this, and I will succeed too.

expectations: Increased resilience to internal and external criticism
Reduced emotional tension
Less fear of making mistakes
